Least
leest
adj., adv., n.
Old English læst, superlative of læssa, less. Webster 1828: smallest; little beyond others, either in size, degree, quantity or dignity. In the Authorized Version least is a kingdom word: it marks where God characteristically starts, and it is the self-description of the men He used most.

Biblical Definition

Least in Scripture is rarely a measurement and almost always a verdict — and the verdict is regularly reversed. Gideon protests that his family is poor and he the least in his father’s house; Saul answers Samuel, Am not I a Benjamite, of the smallest of the tribes of Israel? and my family the least of all the families of the tribe of Benjamin? (1 Samuel 9:21). The Lord makes the pattern a principle: he that is least among you all, the same shall be great (Luke 9:48), and He measures the kingdom’s smallest member against the greatest man born of women — he that is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he (Matthew 11:11). The mustard seed is the least of all seeds: but when it is grown, it is the greatest among herbs (Matthew 13:32). Faithfulness is tested at the same scale: He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much (Luke 16:10), and the commandments are guarded there too, for whoever breaks one of these least commandments and teaches men so shall be called the least in the kingdom (Matthew 5:19). Paul, who had every credential, ends where the pattern ends: I am the least of the apostles (1 Corinthians 15:9), and later, less than the least of all saints (Ephesians 3:8). That is not affectation. It is what grace does to a man’s arithmetic.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines LEAST as smallest; little beyond others, either in size, quantity, degree or dignity; the superlative of little. As an adverb, in the smallest or lowest degree.

expand to see more

LEAST, a. [superl. of little.] — Smallest; little beyond others, either in size, quantity, degree or dignity; as the least insect; the least mercy. LEAST, adv. — In the smallest or lowest degree; in a degree below all others; as, to reward those who least deserve it.

Webster includes dignity among the things a man may be least in, and that is the biblical use. Scripture’s least is usually a ranking rather than a size — the smallest tribe, the youngest son, the last apostle — which is exactly what makes the reversals so pointed.

Key Scripture

Ephesians 3:8 — "Unto me, who am less than the least of all saints, is this grace given, that I should preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ;"

Matthew 25:40 — "And the King shall answer and say unto them, Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me."

Luke 16:10 — "He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much: and he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much."

Matthew 5:19 — "Whosoever therefore shall break one of these least commandments, and shall teach men so, he shall be called the least in the kingdom of heaven: but whosoever shall do and teach them, the same shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven."

1 Corinthians 15:9 — "For I am the least of the apostles, that am not meet to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God."

Modern Corruption

Least is corrupted most often at Matthew 25:40, where the least of these my brethren is detached from the brethren Christ names and made a general warrant for humanitarian activity, and at Matthew 5:19, where least commandments is used to grade God’s law into optional and essential tiers.

expand to see more

The least of these my brethren has become one of the most quoted and least examined phrases in Scripture. In the judgment scene the King identifies a specific group — His brethren, hungry, thirsty, strangers, naked, sick, and in prison — and the nations are judged by their treatment of them. The immediate reference is to Christ’s own people, and the passage is about how the world receives those who bear His name and His message. That reading does not cancel the church’s duty to the poor; Scripture commands mercy to the stranger, the widow, the orphan, and the afflicted in a hundred places, and the Christian who feeds the hungry is obeying God. But when Matthew 25 is made the charter for a general social programme, two things quietly follow: the works are severed from faith in Christ and made the ground of acceptance, and the church’s particular obligation to persecuted believers is diluted into everyone’s obligation to everyone. The verse is stronger, not weaker, when read as it stands.

Matthew 5:19 suffers the opposite handling. These least commandments is read as Christ’s own concession that some commands are minor and may be quietly retired — an assumption that then does considerable work in setting aside whatever a given age finds inconvenient, particularly on sexual order and creational design. But the verse is a warning, not a permission slip: the one who breaks the least commandment and teaches men so shall be called the least in the kingdom of heaven. The Lord is defending the smallest jot and tittle in the very sentence, having just said He came not to destroy the law but to fulfil it. That some commandments are weightier is His own teaching elsewhere; that any are dispensable is precisely what He denies here.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Two Greek superlatives and one Hebrew adjective carry least. The Greek pair distinguishes the absolutely smallest from the merely small, and Paul coins a comparative on the superlative itself in Ephesians 3:8 — a grammatical impossibility used on purpose.

expand to see more

Greek elachistos (G1646) — smallest, least, most insignificant (Matthew 25:40; Luke 16:10; 1 Corinthians 15:9).

Greek mikros (G3398) — small, little, least; the ordinary word for size, and the root of English micro-.

Hebrew qātān (H6996) — small, young, insignificant, least (1 Samuel 9:21, Saul on his own family and tribe).

In Ephesians 3:8 Paul writes a comparative built on a superlative — less than the least, literally leaster. The grammar breaks because the point does.

Usage

"He that is least among you all, the same shall be great (Luke 9:48) — the kingdom’s ranking runs backwards from the world’s."

"Faithful in that which is least (Luke 16:10): the small scale is where fidelity is actually tested."

"Paul moves from the least of the apostles (1 Corinthians 15:9) to less than the least of all saints (Ephesians 3:8) — the direction of a man under grace."
